patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2] mm/mempolicy: recompute automatic interleave weights on memory hotplug

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2] mm/mempolicy: recompute automatic interleave weights on memory hotplug

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance regression caused by outdated automatic interleave weights in the Linux kernel's memory policy module (mm/mempolicy). When nodes gain or lose memory, their weights are not recalculated from their reported bandwidths, leading to an uneven distribution of data and potential overload. The patch introduces a new function, wi_state_refresh(), which recomputes the weights based on the recorded bandwidth whenever a node gains or loses its first/last memory. If allocating new weights fails, it warns once and continues with the next recompute starting from the full bandwidth table.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that the condition in wi_state_refresh() function does not correctly handle cases where old_wi_state is NULL and mode_auto is true, potentially leading to incorrect behavior.

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Andrew Morton noted that the original patch description mentioned that HMAT and CXL report a node's bandwidth only when it first gains memory, but this logic was not correctly applied in the code changes. Specifically, the wi_state_refresh() function should recompute weights whenever N_MEMORY changes, which is already handled by the hotplug notifier. However, the comment also suggests that the original patch description and the code changes are inconsistent, as the original description implies that the weights should be recomputed on every memory hotplug event.
sentiment_signals: inconsistency between patch description and code

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: use one node set for interleave weights

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: use one node set for interleave weights

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a divide error on x86 and panic when memory is being online, caused by torn reads on the nodemask N_MEMORY. It records the nodes visited while summing bandwidth and uses that same set for scaling and reducing weights, ensuring consistent state even if N_MEMORY changes.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn
review_comments.summary: Approved the fix and added a Reviewed-by tag, considering it makes sense to use a consistent node set for interleave weights.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Oct 30, 2026 at 12:12 PM Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:
>
> From: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
>
> From: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
>
> Switching weighted interleave back to automatic mode while memory is
> being onlined can cause a kernel divide error on x86, and a panic if
> panic_on_oops is set.
>
> reduce_interleave_weights() scans N_MEMORY three times, but hotplug
> can cause N_MEMORY to change at runtime - and torn reads on that
> nodemask can cause a total sum of zero bandwidth.  A node that
> was hot-unplugged and then hotplugged back can then cause this
> loop to generate a div/0.
>
> Record the nodes visited while summing their bandwidth, then use
> that same set when scaling and reducing the weights.  This gives
> us a consistent state even if N_MEMORY changes.

Makes a lot of sense to me. Thanks for the fix!
Reviewed-by: Joshua Hahn <joshua.hahnjy@gmail.com>

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] scsi: mpt3sas: Time out delayed not-responding device blocks

version_history.subject: [PATCH] scsi: mpt3sas: Time out delayed not-responding device blocks

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a deadlock issue in the mpt3sas driver where a device is blocked by a DELAY_NOT_RESPONDING event, preventing further scan attempts from proceeding. The patch introduces a delayed work to unblock expired devices after a missing delay period plus an additional 30 seconds. This approach ensures that devices are not stuck waiting for a lock and allows the system to recover from such situations.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 0/6] nfsd: add new export options for controlling read/write iomode

version_history.subject: [PATCH 0/6] nfsd: add new export options for controlling read/write iomode
[PATCH v2 0/6] nfsd: add new export options for controlling read/write iomode

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/6] NFSD: Add per-export read/write I/O mode settings
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds per-export read/write I/O mode settings to the NFS server. It introduces two new fields, 'read-io' and 'write-io', in the struct svc_export to store these settings. The patch also updates the netlink specification to include an io-mode enum and defines NFSD_IO_BUFFERED/DONTCACHE/DIRECT in terms of it. The new options are only accessible through netlink and are parsed on cache update, with their values reported in nfsd.export/content.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/6] NFSD: Apply per-export I/O modes to READ and WRITE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the NFSD code to apply per-export I/O modes to READ and WRITE operations. It resolves each export's effective I/O mode by checking explicit settings or using the global io_cache_read/write knob. The patch also removes unnecessary coupling between debugfs knobs, allowing for more flexible configuration of I/O behavior on a per-export basis. Additionally, it updates debugfs comments to match the new behavior and introduces a global 'never splice' override.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/6] NFSD: Document per-export read_io= and write_io= options
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds documentation for two new export options in the NFS server: read_io= and write_io=. These options allow administrators to set the I/O mode for each export independently, overriding global settings. The options accept three values: buffered, dontcache, or direct, with the same meanings as their corresponding debugfs values. The patch also explains how these per-export settings interact with global knobs and are reported in /proc/net/rpc/nfsd.export/content.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/6] NFSD: Keep per-export statistics across export cache updates
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where per-export statistics in the NFS server are lost when export cache entries are replaced or removed. To solve this, it introduces a new data structure to store these statistics on a per-net basis, keyed by the export root and client name. This allows statistics to be preserved even after cache updates or restarts. A delayed work item is used to free unused statistics after an hour of inactivity.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 5/6] NFSD: Count the storage reads of each export's READs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new counter to track the storage reads of each export in NFS, which is essential for determining the optimal I/O mode for an export. The current implementation only reports bytes returned by READ operations, but this does not accurately reflect the actual storage reads. To address this issue, the patch introduces a new io_read_storage counter that captures the difference between the read_bytes charged to the submitting task and the initial value of read_bytes when a READ operation starts. This approach accounts for readahead and metadata reads, making it applicable to various types of reads. The new counter is only visible with CONFIG_TASK_IO_ACCOUNTING enabled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 6/6] NFSD: Document how to choose an IO mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds documentation to help administrators choose the correct IO mode for an NFS export, including when to use buffered, dontcache, or direct IO. It explains why a low server page cache hit rate is normal and lists workload conditions that favor each IO mode. The document also describes existing metrics to measure performance, such as per-export miss ratio and client mountstats byte counters.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series adds new export options to the NFS server (nfsd) for controlling read and write I/O modes on a per-export basis, replacing global debugfs switches. The options are read_io= and write_io=, which can be set to buffered, direct, or dontcache. This change aims to provide more fine-grained control over I/O behavior and eventually move these controls to something more permanent.

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Chuck Lever questioned the need for randomizing clientids, session IDs, and COPY_NOTIFY tokens, citing that if a client or middlebox is interpreting these values, it's behavior not supported by the protocol specification (RFC 8881). He suggested there may be alternative ways to provide operational needs, such as correlating packet captures with server-side events or diffing traces between runs.
review_comments.raw_body:
I'd like to understand the use case better. Can you say concretely what
consumes the contents of these tokens, and what breaks when they are
random?

The protocol mandates that nothing on the client side should care about
the non-sequence ID parts of these cookies. RFC 8881 defines the client
ID as a server-chosen shorthand (Section 2.4), gives the stateid's
"other" field no meaning beyond identifying a set of locks (Section
8.2.2), and declares sessionid4 as an opaque array. The seqid field is
the one part of a stateid that carries client-visible semantics, and
this series leaves that field alone; it is still a monotonically
increasing integer.

So if a client or a middlebox is interpreting these values, that is
behavior the spec does not support, and I'm not inclined to add a knob
to accommodate it. On the other hand, if the need is operational, say
correlating packet captures with server-side events or diffing traces
between runs, there may be a better way to provide that than
predictable tokens.


-- 
Chuck Lever (Come to NFS bake-a-thon! https://nfsv4bat.org)
